opus-5.5.text:
I think language models are remarkable, and I want to start by giving them real credit. Language is an incredibly efficient medium. It's something humans built over thousands of years to compress what we know about the world into a form we can share. So when you train a model on huge amounts of text, you're getting a highly distilled, curated summary of human knowledge and reasoning. That's why LLMs are so good at abstraction, planning, symbolic reasoning, and communication. In a sense, language is a cheat code: someone has already done much of the hard work of turning raw experience into concepts.

But that's also the limitation. Language is a description of the world. It isn't the world. It's a low-bandwidth, lossy projection of reality. A lot of what we understand never gets written down, because it's so obvious to us that nobody bothers. How objects fall, how liquid pours, how a room looks when you turn your head, how hard you need to grip a cup. A child learns that from seeing and touching things long before they can talk. Text only captures the residue of that knowledge, filtered through what humans thought was worth saying.

So my view is that if you build a world model on language alone, you inherit those blind spots. The model can talk fluently about physics without having any grounded sense of space, continuity, or cause and effect. You see it when you ask these models to reason about spatial relationships, or to predict what happens next in a video. They often fail in ways that are almost alien, because they're pattern-matching on descriptions rather than modeling the underlying dynamics.

That's why I've cared so much about vision and, more broadly, about sensory, embodied data. Visual data is much higher bandwidth and much less curated. It's messier, and it's harder to learn from, because nobody has pre-digested it for you. But it's closer to the actual structure of the world. I think a real world model needs to learn representations directly from that kind of signal: space, time, physics, object permanence. Language should sit on top as an interface, a way to reason and communicate, rather than being the foundation.

It's a bit like Plato's cave. Language models are learning from very detailed shadows on the wall, and they've become extraordinarily good at that. But at some point you want to turn around and look at the thing casting the shadows. I don't think scaling text will get us there. It's a different research problem, and frankly I think it's one of the most exciting open problems in AI right now.

r001.rationale: The response says models are trained on text and learn from descriptions, but does not characterize language as the model’s target or supervision space.

r002.rationale: It says language is a lossy description that omits much unstated knowledge and that text captures only a residue of what people know.

r003.rationale: It describes language as a medium for sharing human knowledge and communication, but does not identify human alignment as an advantage that language already provides.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think language models are an incredible starting point, but I'd push back on the idea that they're a sufficient foundation for a world model on their own.

Let me start with the strengths, because they're real. Language is humanity's compression of experience. When you train on the entire internet, you're inheriting an enormous amount of structured knowledge about how the world works, encoded by billions of people over centuries. That's why LLMs can reason about physics, about causality, about social dynamics, without ever having seen or touched anything. They've learned from our descriptions of it. And the scaling story with language has been remarkably clean. Next-token prediction turned out to be a surprisingly rich objective. So as a knowledge substrate and as a reasoning engine, language models are far ahead of anything we have in vision or embodied AI.

But here's the limitation I keep coming back to. Language is a lossy, low-bandwidth channel. Humans wrote down what was worth writing down, which means the training data is heavily biased toward things that are surprising, abstract, or socially useful. Nobody writes a blog post about how a cup looks when you rotate it thirty degrees, or how shadows fall as the sun moves, or what happens to the water level when you tilt a glass. That stuff is so obvious to us that it never gets verbalized. And yet that's exactly what a world model needs to capture: continuous physical structure, spatial relationships, the geometry and dynamics of the actual world.

When I look at the multimodal LLMs we have now, a lot of them are essentially language models with a visual tokenizer bolted on. The visual information gets squeezed through a bottleneck and the language backbone does the thinking. And they're genuinely bad at things that are trivially easy for a five-year-old: counting objects, telling left from right, judging relative depth, reading a clock. Not because the models aren't smart, but because the visual representation was never pushed to be good at those things. The language side carries the model, and the vision side is treated as an afterthought.

So my view is that a world model built purely on language is, in a sense, building on the shadows rather than the objects. Language gives you the abstractions, but you need a strong perceptual and spatial foundation underneath it, learned from pixels and video and interaction, where the model has to actually understand structure rather than retrieve a description of it. The question I find most interesting is how to combine the two, so that the language model's reasoning is grounded in representations that actually encode the world, not just what people said about it.

r001.rationale: It mentions training on internet text and next-token prediction, but does not characterize language models as operating in the target or supervision space.

r002.rationale: It says language is a lossy, low-bandwidth channel that omits unspoken physical details such as continuous structure, spatial relationships, and dynamics.

r003.rationale: It describes knowledge encoded in language, but does not identify alignment with humans as an advantage of using language.

astra-6.text:
I think language models give us a very powerful starting point, because language contains so much of what humans have learned about the world. We describe objects, relationships, causes and effects, even things we’ve never directly experienced. Learning from that gives a model access to an enormous amount of accumulated knowledge.

But I would distinguish between learning how we describe the world and learning how the world actually behaves. Language is selective. When I describe picking up a cup, I leave out almost everything about the geometry, the forces, the movement of my fingers. Those details are obvious to us because we have perception and experience. They’re not necessarily recoverable from the description alone.

So the question is what we expect a world model to do. If we want it to answer questions or reason about familiar situations, language can take us very far. If we want it to predict what happens when an agent acts in a physical environment, then grounding becomes much more important. It needs observations, actions, and feedback that can correct its predictions.

I wouldn’t frame this as language versus vision. Vision also gives you an incomplete picture. The interesting direction is connecting these sources of information: language provides abstractions, perception provides evidence, and interaction lets you test whether your understanding is right. Language models can be a major component of that system, but I wouldn’t assume that language alone is a sufficient foundation.

r001.rationale: The response discusses learning from language and its limits, but does not characterize language models as operating in the target or supervision space of machine learning.

r002.rationale: It says some physical details are omitted from descriptions and may not be recoverable from them alone. It does not state that those aspects cannot be represented through language.

r003.rationale: The response says language contains accumulated human knowledge, but does not identify alignment with humans as an advantage of using language itself.

sol-6.1.text:
I think language is an incredibly powerful source of supervision, because so much human knowledge is expressed through language. By learning to predict text, a model can acquire a lot of structure about the world: relationships between concepts, common patterns, even some ability to reason. So I wouldn’t dismiss language modeling as just learning correlations between words.

But I would separate a model of what people say about the world from a model of how the world actually works. Those overlap, but they’re not identical. A lot of physical knowledge never gets written down because, for humans, it’s obvious. You learn it by seeing, moving, touching things, and observing what happens when you take an action.

For example, you can describe an object falling in a sentence, but that description leaves out most of the visual and physical detail. And being able to explain what should happen doesn’t necessarily mean you can predict it reliably in a new situation.

So I see language as a very important component, but I’m less convinced that it should be the sole foundation. We need models that can learn from perception and interaction, and connect that experience to language. The interesting question is how to bring those sources of information together so that the model’s understanding is grounded in the world.

r001.rationale: It describes language as a source of supervision and says models learn by predicting text.

r002.rationale: It says much physical knowledge is never written down and that language descriptions omit visual and physical detail.

r003.rationale: It notes that human knowledge is expressed through language, but does not identify alignment with humans as an advantage of using language.
